Quarter sized hail was reported 2 miles south of Sadler.
Ping pong ball sized hail was reported near downtown Dallas.
Large tree branches were broken off and wood fences were knocked down just southeast of downtown Dallas.
The automated weather station at Arlington Municipal Airport (KGKY) measured a 70 MPH wind gust.
The automated weather station at North Texas Regional Airport (KGYI) measured a 58 MPH wind gust.
Quarter to golfball sized hail fell just east of Sherman.
Quarter sized hail was reported 7 miles south of Rhome or near Pecan Acres in northwest Tarrant County.
Large tree limbs were knocked down in Celina.
The automated weather station at North Texas Regional Airport (KGYI) measured a 62 MPH wind gust.

Thunderstorm winds were estimated to be 65 MPH in Richardson.
A 62 MPH wind gust was measured near the intersection of Highway 78 and CR 549 on the east side of Lake Lavon. Power flashes were also reported.
Large trees were knocked down in Highland Park.
Seventy MPH wind gusts were estimated in Kaufman at Highway 243 and Highway 175.
A brief tornado was reported 2 miles southeast of St. Jo near Highway 82. Some tree damage was reported. This tornado was rated an EF-0 with maximum estimated winds of 70 MPH.
A brief tornado touched down on the east side of Lake Nocona. No damage was reported with this tornado. Maximum winds were estimated to be 70 MPH with this tornado.
A brief tornado was observed about 3 miles north of Rhome. Some minor damage was reported to barns, and this tornado was rated an EF-0 with maximum estimated winds of 75-80 MPH.

A tornado was observed approximately 1.5 miles northwest of Sanctuary along Spring Valley Court. The roof of a mobile home was damaged and trees were damaged along the path of the tornado. Panels were torn off the roof of the mobile home and tossed into the back yard. This tornado was rated an EF-0 with maximum estimated winds of 85 MPH.
A waterspout was observed over Lake Worth, and then it moved onto land damaging trees along Boat Club Road on the east side of the lake.

A NWS Storm Survey determined that a EF-2 tornado began near the Argyle/Denton city line and traveled northeast for just over 1 mile. The tornado began in the Country Lakes subdivision where it significantly damaged the roofs of numerous homes. At least 10 to 12 homes sustained moderate damage. However, two homes lost part of their roofs on the order of EF-2 damage. To the northeast of the subdivision, near Johnson Lane, another home sustained minor roof damage and a barn was destroyed. Trees were also damaged along the path of the tornado. Maximum winds with this tornado were estimated between 115 and 125 MPH.

A NWS Storm Survey determined that an EF-1 tornado occurred in the city of Irving, south of Highway 183. This tornado began along West Grauwyler Road and traveled nearly due south about one and a third miles before lifting near Story Road and 5th Street. Significant tree damage occurred in the Sherwood Forest neighborhood and some roofs were damaged in the same neighborhood. Most of the damage occurred south of Conflans Road along Huntington Drive. One large tree fell through the second story of a home. A small apartment complex at the end of Highland Park Drive was also significantly damaged. The roof was partially torn off one building, and the chimney and A/C vents were also torn off the same roof. Roof damage was observed on other apartment buildings and many windows were broken. South of the apartment complex, across Rock Island Road, the metal roof of a small retail building was torn off, and other buildings in the same retail center sustained damage. Significant tree damage also occurred along the southern portions of the tornado track. Maximum estimated winds were 105 MPH.

A NWS Storm Survey determined that straight-line winds damaged several trees at an apartment complex in the Oak Lawn area of Dallas, located southeast of Dallas Love Field Airport (KDAL). Power lines were also knocked down, and a man died of electrocution from the fallen power lines. It is believed he went outside after the storm had passed and was electrocuted by the power line laying on the ground, possibly hidden under a fallen tree branch or leaves.

A truck carrying eight people hit standing water on the eastbound lanes of I-30 and lost control. The vehicle flipped over the guardrail and traveled another 200 feet before stopping. A 20 year old male passenger was killed and 5 others were transported to the hospital.

Due to several supercells moving across the county, several trees and power poles were knocked down around the county.

The roof was blown off an unoccupied school in Chico. A few trees were also knocked down across the county.

Trees were uprooted and snapped in Decatur. The golden arches at McDonald's were knocked down, and the Dairy Queen and Taco Bell signs were also damaged along with other business signs in the city. Power lines were also knocked down and shingles were torn off roofs. A home weather station on Highway 287 on the north side of town measured a 62 MPH wind gust. A 50 foot hackberry tree, the largest in the county, was knocked down in Decatur by the storm, and it fell on a garage, crushing the car underneath.

Hail up to the size of quarters fell at Mayhill Road and I-35E in southeast Denton.
Lightning struck a pallet company in Hewitt located on the 7300 block of Bagby Avenue. Several pallets caught on fire.

An EF-0 tornado occurred in White Settlement east of Loop 820 and south of White Settlement Road. Initially, tree limbs and fences were knocked down and minor roof damage was observed. The tornado then traveled into Central Park where it snapped at least three light poles and destroyed a storage shed. A convergent pattern to the damage helped verify the occurrence of a brief tornado. Maximum estimated winds were 75 to 85 MPH.

A rain-wrapped, EF-0 tornado damaged one home and several trees on the west and north sides of Lake Kiowa. Trees were partially uprooted and one home had a portion of its roof removed. At least 20 other homes sustained minor roof and shingle damage. Maximum estimated winds were 75 to 85 MPH with this tornado. Damaging straight-line winds damaged other trees around the lake.
An EF-0 tornado occurred approximately 9 miles northeast of Jacksboro. This tornado damaged trees with maximum estimated winds around 80 MPH.

Tennis ball sized hail was reported 2 miles east of Graham.

A trained spotter reported 74 MPH winds in Bridgeport.

Sections of the roof of the Sunset Inn in Decatur were blown off by thunderstorm winds. One person was injured by falling debris and was transported to the hospital.

Severe thunderstorm winds tore the roof off of Ojedas Mexican Restaurant in Lewisville. The roof was blown into an apartment complex behind the restaurant.

Lightning started a house fire in the 2000 block of Northridge in Forney.
A 52-year old male died in Fort Worth due to heat. He was found in his vehicle during the late afternoon hours. He had no underlying health problems that also contributed to his death.

The medical examiner ruled a 21-year old male, a 43-year old male and a 50-year old male all died from hyperthermia in Dallas County. The 21-year old male was found inside a home on the 28th when temperatures were around 99 degrees.The 50-year old male was found in his home on the 19th when temperatures were around 103 degrees. The 43-year old male was found in the garage of his home on the 20th when temperatures were around 100 degrees. A heat advisory was not in effect on any of these days. Also during the month of June, the Dallas County Health & Human Services reported 140 cases of heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke.

A significant microburst occurred in the city of Muenster. Numerous trees were uprooted across the city, the field house of a school was damaged, a church sustained substantial damage, several roofs were torn off homes, mobile homes suffered significant damage, and tombstones at the local cemetery were blown over and crushed. The most costly damage occurred to two grain silos. Along Main Street, many businesses were heavily damaged and the windows were blown out of Orr Construction. The damage across the city was estimated to total over 1 million dollars.
Gutters and pieces of siding were torn off a home in Lindsay. A glass table was also picked up, shattered, and blown into a pool.
Large trees were blown across roadways south of Gainesville.

Multiple trees were blown down due to high thunderstorm winds 2 miles east of Gainesville. One tree fell on a home and resulted in one minor injury to the occupant of the house.

High winds caused substantial damage to a home in Sadler. A person inside the home suffered a broken arm. There was also damage to several outbuildings, two metal barns suffered roof damage, and many large trees were blown down.

A 230 acre blaze burned from approximately Waxahachie in Ellis County to DeSoto in Dallas County. In Ellis County, one home was burned in Glenn Heights, five cars were destroyed, and 12 other homes were damaged. Most of the damaged homes were also in Glenn Heights or in Red Oak. Four power poles were also burned. Two fire fighters were treated for heat exhaustion while battling the blaze.

A wildfire in Young County burned 600 acres. The fire began near FM 578 and Carmax Road. Only 1 mile of flow line was destroyed.
A 300-acre fire in the Troy-Pendleton area burned approximately 200 round bales of hay.

Business signs were blown down on Grand Avenue.
Trees and tree limbs were blown down due to strong thunderstorm winds in Waco.

Triple digit temperatures were recorded 30 out of 31 days during the month of July. According to the medical examiner, a total of 9 people died as a result of the heat. Most of the deceased were over the age of 65 and all but one were found inside their homes. All of deaths occurred after the 14th. In addition, the medical examiner reported 223 cases of heat-related illness were treated in the county during the month. A heat advisory was in effect from the 11th through the 18th, and then again from the 23rd through the 31st.

Triple digit temperatures were recorded nearly every day during the month of July. A 4-year old died inside a vehicle on the 11th. Temperatures on this day were at or slightly above 100 degrees. A heat advisory was in effect from the 11th through the 18th, and then again from the 23rd through the 31st.

Temperatures this month ranged from the upper 90s to over 100 degrees during the month of July. An elderly women died in her overheated home on the 7th, and a second heat victim was found outside on the 15th while working on a job. A heat advisory was in effect from the 11th through the 18th, and then again from the 23rd through the 31st.

Triple digit temperatures were recorded nearly every day during the month of July. On the 9th, a female crashed her all-terrain vehicle while riding on a deer lease and became disoriented in the heat while trying to walk for help. The medical examiner determined she died from heat exhaustion. A heat advisory was not in effect on this day, but temperatures were around 104 degrees.

The chimney of a home on Knowles Road near Ogelsby was knocked off the home by strong thunderstorm winds.  A tractor and three cars on the property were also damaged. The carport at his neighbor's house was blown across the yard.
Metal roofs were torn off buildings at the Morton Salt Mine located southeast of town. Some minor roof damage was also reported in Grand Saline.
Fourteen inch diameter trees were knocked down 2 miles north of Concord Church along County Road 404.
The roof was blown off a manufactured home west of Tennessee Colony.
Trees up to 12 inches in diameter were knocked down in Honey Grove. Two of these trees fell on homes. Power lines were also knocked down.

A microburst caused damage to two barns and a manufactured home at County Roads 2194 and 1025 north of Farmersville. The roofs of both barns were torn off and the metal covering of the roof of the manufactured home was peeled back. One of the barns had a tin metal roof and the tin was twisted around a pole. The other barn had a plywood roof with shingles. In addition, a power pole was leaning on the property.
Trees were knocked down in the Montalba area.

Medium sized trees were knocked down along FM 3236 north-northeast of Sulphur Springs. Some sheds were also displaced several yards along the same road. One residential home on FM 3236 sustained damage. The damage was the result of a microburst from a dissipating, high-based thunderstorm.
Dime sized hail was reported on Highway 155 between Frankston and Palestine.
Part of the roof of a manufactured home in Pert was removed. Another part of the roof was partially lifted off the home.
Trees were blown down on FM 315 approximately 10 miles north of Palestine. One of the trees was 15 inches in diameter.
Nickel sized hail fell 8 miles west-northwest of Palestine.
Large pine trees were knocked down approximately 2-3 miles south of Tennessee Colony on FM 645. Some trees fell across FM 645.
A few hail stones up to the size of quarters fell in Grand Saline.

A grass fire that started in the 11000 block of East Dawn Drive in far north Fort Worth, spread quickly and consumed 5 mobile homes. At least one shed and a car were also engulfed in the flames. Power poles also caught fire causing the power lines to fall. One firefighter suffered first degree burns on his hands and another was treated for heat exhaustion.

The CR 156 Fire began July 26th approximately 16 miles south of Breckenridge near Highway 183. The fire was first contained on July 28th after burning a total of 4321 acres. Two homes, two deer shelters, a vehicle, and an outbuilding were lost in the fire. On August 4th, this fire reignited and consumed another 614 acres for a final total of 4935 acres. The fire was finally completely controlled on August 14th.

The Armstrong Fire began July 12th approximately 6 miles north of Bryson near FM 1191 and Berwick Road. The fire was controlled on July 14th and burned approximately 700 acres. The fire was started by logging equipment. No structures or homes were lost or damaged by this fire.
A wildfire burned approximately 500 acres in western Grayson County. The fire began near State Highway 56 and O'Hanlon Road, west of Southmayd. One barn and one power pole was damaged.

A grass fire began on July 4th approximately 5 miles northwest of Mineral Wells. This fire was contained on July 15th and burned a total of 932 acres. A camper and some outbuildings were lost in the fire. On the 7th, a firefighter from Boise, ID died due to hyperthermia while working on the lines of the 337 Fire.
A 125-acre blaze between South Keller Road and Glidewell Road, east of Mineral Wells, burned two abandoned houses and a shed. The fire was started by lightning.
A small grass fire in Mineral Wells burned a shed.

A grass fire began on July 3rd approximately 7 miles southwest of Rio Vista. This fire was contained on the 4th but briefly reignited on the 5th burning 5 more acres. This fire burned a total of 750 acres.

The Highway 6 Fire began July 26th approximately 2 miles north of Cisco. The fire was contained on July 27th and burned approximately 50 acres; however, 3 large outbuildings and a backhoe were lost in this fire.

The CR 156 Fire began July 26th approximately 16 miles south of Breckenridge near Highway 183. The fire was first contained on July 28th after burning a total of 4321 acres. Two homes, two deer shelters, a vehicle, and an outbuilding were lost in the fire. On August 4th, this fire reignited and consumed another 614 acres for a final total of 4935 acres. During the rekindle, another home, vehicle, a barn, and several more outbuildings were lost. The fire was finally completely controlled on August 14th.

The Gunn Road Fire began in the early evening hours of July 13th along FM 917 just southwest of Joshua. Two grass fires were intentionally set by an arsonist, and the fire merged into one blaze. The fire burned 80 acres, was contained on the evening of the 13th, and controlled on the evening of the 15th. One vacant home was lost in this fire, another structure was also lost, and one firefighter was hospitalized for heat exhaustion.
A grass fire near Pump Station Road and Highway 79 burned 5 acres. The fire destroyed 3 abandoned structures and damaged 1 other structure.
A grass fire burned 202 acres north of Adamsville near County Roads 2901 & 2925. This fire burned 1 structure, was contained on the 21st and controlled on the 22nd.

Strong downburst winds from a summertime thunderstorm knocked down small trees and tree limbs in Cheneyboro. The storm also produced small hail around 0.50 in diameter, and the hail damaged the sides of homes and awnings.
Strong downburst winds from a summertime thunderstorm knocked down a few power poles and caused minor roof damage to one home on County Road 4043 south of Kemp.
A grass fire broke out on FM 156 north of Eastland. The fire damaged power lines and burned a tank battery.

The Coryell Complex was a group of 11 grass fires that were started approximately 4 miles southeast of Evant along US Highway 84 and FM 183. The 11 fires eventually merged into 5 fires that were managed as a complex. A vehicle towing a barbecue pit was believed to have started the fires which began on August 28th, was contained on September 1st, and fully controlled on September 14th. A total of 1635 acres burned. The largest fire burned approximately 1400 acres.
The Gage Fire started approximately 9 miles northwest of Sherman, near Highway 82. The fire burned approximately 3840 acres and 2 large barns.

The Robinette Fire started 11 miles north-northwest of Killeen on the Fort Hood military base. It started near the East Range Road impact area and burned 6180 acres. The fire began on the 20th, was contained on the 22nd, but was not fully controlled until October 11th.

The Campsey Fire began approximately 11 miles north of Jacksboro just west of Old Postoak Road. The fire burned approximately 2600 acres. Two local firefighters were treated for heat related illnesses while working this fire.

The Jack Mountain fire began on August 30th and was controlled September 14th. The fire began in the Jack Mountain impact area on Fort Hood and burned approximately 3700 acres. The fire was believed to have been started by artillery training exercises, and the only damage reported was to two power poles.

The 101 Ranch fire began on August 30th south of Possum Kingdom Lake on the east side of Highway 16. The fire burned to the north, jumped the highway and burned into the Gaines Bend and Cliffs Subdivisions. It was finally controlled on October 11th after burning 6555 acres. The fire burned 39 homes in the Cliffs and Gaines Bend. The guard shack, the pro shop, and the front office to the Cliffs also burned, and nine recreational vehicles were lost in the fire. One person suffered minor burns and two firefighters sustained minor ankle injuries.

The Horseshoe Bend Fire began on August 26th in far eastern Coryell County near the Leon River. The fire was contained on September 2nd and fully controlled on September 4th. The fire burned 525 acres. One firefighter suffered mild heat exhaustion and another suffered an ankle injury. A bulldozer owned by the Texas Forestry Service was burn in this fire.

The Mustang Fire in Johnson County burned 336 acres, but burned 3 homes and a barn. Two of the homes were destroyed and the third one was damaged. The fire began on the 18th approximately 4 miles northeast of Godley along CR 912, and was controlled on the 20th. Two firefighters were treated for heat exhaustion.

The Cherry Homes fire burned approximately 7328 acres of range land. It started approximately 13 miles northeast of Jacksboro at Cundiff Crafton Road. The fire started on the 7th from a campfire, was contained on the 10th, and controlled on the 14th. A travel trailer and a barn were destroyed in the fire.
The Post Oak Fire began on August 1st, was contained on the 3rd, and fully controlled on the 4th. The fire started approximately 9 miles north of Jacksboro and burned 571 acres.

The Penial Fire burned in the northwest side of Greenville, inside an area contained by US 69 to the west, Dell St to the north, Reese St to the east, and Lee Street to the south. The fire started on the afternoon of the 18th and was controlled on the afternoon of the 21st. It burned a total of 250 acres including 2 large barns, 2 small outbuildings, and 3 cars. This fire was one of about a dozen grass fires that occurred in the Greenville area on this afternoon. All the other grass fires burned smaller acreage, but a few storage sheds were burned in the other fires.

The Boat Fire began approximately 3.5 miles southeast of Celeste near CR 1040 and CR 1037. The fire began on the 18th and was controlled on the 21st. The fire burned approximately 100 acres and burned into a boat junk yard. Approximately 25 unused junk boats and many old vehicle tires burned in the fire.

Fire #338/Mackie Ranch Fire burned approximately 25 acres, but burned one outbuilding. The fire burned near FM 637 approximately 2 miles to the northeast of Mildred. The cause of the fire was electrical.

The 3547 Fire burned approximately 400 acres and was controlled September 6th. The fire was ignited by farm equipment along CR 3547 approximately 6 miles southwest of Paradise. Five homes, 3 outbuildings, a ranch barn, 1 tractor, and several hay bales were lost in the fire. One person was injured and transported to a hospital.

A fire that broke out on Dick Price Road near Rendon consumed three houses. The embers from this fire started another fire that burned a fourth home on Swiney Hiett Road in Kennedale, and then the fire damaged a warehouse and two unoccupied trailer homes on Eden Road.

A tree limb fell on a power line and sparked a grass fire the burned 464 acres near Todd City. The Todd City fire was centered near the intersection of FM 19 and CR 335 in the northeastern part of the county. The fire began on the 15th, was contained on the 15th, and then fully controlled on the 20th. The fire consumed a deer camp, a fiberglass salt water tank, several outbuildings, and an oil tank. One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion and smoke inhalation and was taken to the hospital.
A small acre fire just off Hwy 36 in Rogers destroyed a vacant mobile home. It was believed that a piece of farm equipment may have sparked the fire.

The Pilot Knob fire burned 1500 acres on the Fort Hood military base. This fire was also located on the firing range, approximately 6 miles away from the Robinette Fire, and was started by training exercises on the range. The fire began on the 20th, was contained on the 22nd, but was not fully controlled until October 11th.
A blown tire started a fire along Interstate 30 near Ranger Hill. The fire burned 1320 acres. This fire began on the 12th, was contained on the 15th, and then fully controlled on the 24th.
Fire #695 burned 6 acres approximately 3 miles west of Centerville. The fire burned a 2-story house and a shed. The fire was started by debris burning.
A small acre fire consumed two vacant mobile homes near FM 914 and FM 847, approximately 3.5 miles south of Stephenville.

A grass fire damaged a group of vacant manufactured homes off Jimmy Lane in Combine. One home was destroyed and five others were badly damaged. Only one of the homes was occupied at the time. A few vehicles and some sheds were also burned in the fire.

A small 2-acre grass fire near CRs 917 and 918 burned 62 round bales of hay. This fire was located just east of Cresson and was started by an electrical line. One firefighter had to be transported for heat exhaustion.
A 30-35 acre fire on CR 4765 in Kempner destroyed a vacant home and three other structures. The fire began when a buzzard on an electrical transformer caused the transformer to short out.
A 20-acre grass fire near CR 4820 in Kempner destroyed a mobile home.
A 100-acre grass fire burned along Highway 183 between Watson and Briggs. A live wire started the fire which burned a truck on the property.
A 30-acre fire on CR 3830 in Adamsville burned several metal barns, two cars, and some farm equipment.
A 60-acre fire in Kempner on CR 4772 off FM 2657 burned one car.
A 500-acre fire started near West Moonlight Drive and Losik Road in Robinson. The fire forced the closure of the northbound lane of I-35 but otherwise no structures were damaged.

A 1701-acre grass fire started in Center City along Hwy 84 by a car that likely blew a tire. The blaze began on the 5th, was contained on the 6th, and the fully controlled on the 8th. The fire burned two houses, 8 mobile homes, two sheds, several other barns, and some bales of round hay.
A half acre grass fire near FM 979 in Calvert burned two abandoned houses.
A small fire near Hemphill Street and Loop 820 in southern Tarrant County burned a few bales of hay.
A small fire on CR 1110, between Grand Saline and Canton, burned a barn, a shed, and some abandoned vehicles. The fire was likely started by fireworks.

A small 5-acre fire in the 7800 block of Silverado Loop in Kaufman burned a home.
A 1-acre fire in a subdivision near Farm to Market 753 and County Road 1111 burned a storage structure. The location is approximately 6 miles southwest of Athens.
Penny sized hail was reported 5 miles NE of Nocona.
A lightning strike started a house fire on Axminster Court by White Rock Lake.  The damage to the 5400 square home was estimated around $200,000.
A 2-acre grass fire was intentionally set near South Sycamore Street, south of Palestine. This fire burned a home.

Henderson Fire #475 began on the 30th in the far northeastern parts of the county near Frankston, was contained September 5th, and fully controlled on September 15th. The fire burned 2314 acres and claimed 3 homes.
Penny-sized hail was reported in Oak Ridge.
Nickel-sized hail was reported in Callisburg.
Quarter to golfball-sized hail fell in Oak Ridge.

The 3547 Fire in Wise County began on August 31st and was finally controlled September 6th. The fire burned a total of 400 acres including five homes, 3 outbuildings, a ranch barn, 1 tractor, and several hay bales. Most of the damages occurred on August 31st, and damage estimates for this fire can be found with the initial entry in the August Storm Data report.

The 101 Ranch fire began on August 30th, burned through the month of September, and was finally controlled on October 11th after burning 6555 acres. The fire burned 39 homes in the Cliffs and Gaines Bend. The guard shack, the pro shop, and the front office to the Cliffs also burned, and nine recreational vehicles were lost in the fire. Damage estimates for this fire can be found with the initial entry in the August Storm Data report.

The Horseshoe Bend Fire began on August 26th, was contained on September 2nd and fully controlled on September 4th. The fire burned 525 acres. Damages estimates for this fire can be found with the initial entry in the August Storm Data report.

According to the Texas DEM, a one-acre fire on CR 4343 near LaRue damaged a large shop.

An engine working at a drilling rig site started a large grass fire that burned 1150 acres. This fire was located near FM 1125 and Turkey Ranch Road approximately 7 miles south-southeast of Bowie. No structures were damaged by this fire, but one vehicle was destroyed.

An 18-acre grass fire along FM 314 south of Brownsboro heavily damaged a house. This fire was started along the roadway from a discarded cigarette. The fire was quickly contained on the 3rd but not fully controlled until the 14th.

The Naylor Fire began near Plainview Road and Naylor Road to the southwest of the North Texas Regional Airport. This fire was started on the 3rd by a car and burned 500 acres. It was contained on the 4th and controlled on the 6th.
The Cedar Ridge Fire burned 958 acres between FM 2114 and FM 2490 south of Lake Whitney. The fire began from a vehicle hauling a bar-b-que pit. One camper trailer was damaged by this fire.

Henderson #495 Fire, also known as the New Chapel Fire, burned 5000 acres. This fire was located near FMs 315 and 321 approximately 9 miles north of Palestine. Five barns and 100 bales of hay were lost in this fire.
The Prairie Hill Fire burned 3000 acres around the community of Prairie Hill. This fire was started by downed power lines. The fire was contained on the 4th but not fully controlled until the 14th.

The Concord-Robbins Fire was started on the 4th, contained on the 7th, and fully controlled on the 11th. It burned a total of 4689 acres within an area bordered by FM 39 to the east, FM 1147 to the west and Highway 7 to the north. The fire burned 31 homes, several more sheds and outbuildings, and some farm equipment.

The South Sulphur Fire burned 100 acres near CR 4415 and FM 1566. Two abandoned, unoccupied homes were lost along with 3 barns and 4 large rolls of hay. The fire began and was contained on the 4th but was not fully controlled until the 6th.
The Texas DEM reports a 100-acre fire on CR 367 burned two recreational vehicles.
The Texas DEM reported a 6-acre fire at FM 314 and CR 3603 south of Brownsboro damaged a structure.
A 440-acre fire at FM 148 and CR 2613 near Lively destroyed one home.
The Oak Street Fire in Corsicana burned 30 acres and consumed 9 metal buildings which were shops of small business owners. Fourteen cars were also lost in this fire.

Henderson #507 Fire burned 1400 acres and was started by power lines. This fire began near FM 322 and CR 2109 west of Elkhart. The fire began on the 5th, was contained on the 6th and controlled on the 15th.
Henderson #504 Fire burned 503 acres and burned one home. This fire began near FM 228 and CR 1214 in the far southeastern corner of the county. This fire was started by a downed power line.

Five fires in Freestone County erupted on the 4th. The fires burned a total of 7500 acres. According to the Limestone Office of Emergency Management, 7 homes and 18 outbuildings were burned by these fires. The largest fire was located near Teague and the fire were contained the morning of the 7th.

According to the Texas DEM, 8 fires erupted along Highway 31E near CR 3710 between Athens and Murchison. These fires were likely started by a travel trailer. The fires burned 100 acres and heavily damaged a barn and one other structure.

The Dam Fire on the south edge of Lake Whitney burned 580 acres near the Hill/Bosque County line. Nine homes and 25 outbuildings were lost in the fire. This fire began on the roadside next to SH 22 but the cause was unknown. One firefighter was treated for smoke inhalation.
A grass fire near FM 1188 north of Huckabay burned in a hay field. This fire burned 5-10 acres.
The Texas DEM reported a 4-acre grass fire on FM 3062 near Malakoff burned 4 rows of storage buildings.
A 10-acre fire on Shelby Road between Everman and Kennedale burned two structures. One civilian was injured and treated at the scene.
A 30-acre fire on Retta-Mansfield Road near Mansfield burned 10 outbuildings.
The Texas DEM reported a 70-80 acre fire at J.W. Martine Road near US Highway 79 in the Elliott community burned 20 round bales of hay and a full hay barn.
Thunderstorm wind speeds were estimated to be between 50 and 60 MPH.

A roof was blown of a house and a trailer was blown across Highway 81 at Polk Road. Just up the road near Highway 81 and Indian Hills Road, a large tree was uprooted and several large, healthy tree branches were snapped off a tree.
Tree limbs with a diameter between 6 and 8 inches were blown down in Montague.
A 59 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at Alliance Airport.
A 61 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at Meacham Airport.

Trees were blown down onto homes off of Roberts Cut Off Road in River Oaks. Damage also occurred to businesses along River Oaks Boulevard. A bank drive-thru was damaged, the roof of a barbershop was partially peeled back, the windows were knocked out of a grocery store, a restaurant had its sign twisted, and a clinic lost part of its roof.
Fences and large tree branches were blown down near the intersection of Highway 377 and Farm-to-Market Road 2871 in southwest Benbrook.
A 60 MPH wind gust was estimated at Interstate 35 and Dowdy Ferry Road.
A spotter measured a 63 MPH wind gust at the intersection of Westmoreland Road and Pleasant Run Road in DeSoto.
A 60 MPH wind gust was measured in Red Oak.
Wind speeds were estimated to be 60 MPH near the Cleburne Municipal Airport.
Large branches were blown down about 8 miles east-southeast of Cleburne.
Several trees were blown down in Belton. Thunderstorm winds were estimated to be about 60 mph.
Several trees were blown down and power flashes were also seen in Temple. Thunderstorm wind speeds were estimated to be near 65 MPH.
A 67 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at the Temple Airport.
A 58 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at the Corsicana Airport.
The Crowell Road Fire burned 200 acres near I-30 and CR 2509. Four outbuildings were burned in this fire. The fire was located approximately 13 miles southwest of Greenville.
The Levita Fire burned 60 acres on an exotic game ranch along CR 101, approximately 3 miles west of Levita. One structure was lost in this fire.

The Union Grove Fire was located near Stillhouse Hollow Lake along CR 2484 by Union Grove Park. The fire started when a transformer exploded causing a power line to drop. The fire threatened the South Shores, River's Bend and Woods of Salado developments, and burned 500 acres.
The Ike Road Fire burned 200 acres near Ike Road and FM 879, east of Waxahachie. The fire was started by mowing equipment and burned a travel trailer, a truck, and a boat.
Nickel-sized hail was reported 3 miles south of Gorman.
Several trees were blown down in Ambrose due to high winds.
Power lines were blown down and outbuildings were damaged in Allen due to high winds.
Quarter-sized hail fell at the intersection of Highway 75 and Park Blvd.
Thunderstorm winds gusted up to 60 MPH.
Half dollar-sized hail fell at the intersection of Interstate 635 and Royal Lane.
Quarter-sized hail fell at the intersection of Interstate 635 and Highway 86.
Multiple trees were blown down due to high winds about 5 miles south of Cumby.
Golfball-sized hail fell at the intersection of Interstate 635 and Royal Lane.
Powerlines and a large tree blocked a highway about 4 miles southwest of Sulphur Springs.
A 10-15 acre fire in the 1100 block of Knob Hill Road burned a mobile home. This fire was located approximately 3 miles northwest of Rogers.
A 600-acre fire burned near Oil Field Road in the far southeastern portions of the county. No damage or injuries were reported.
A 15-acre fire near SH 31 and Highway 175 in Athens moderately damaged 2 unoccupied mobile homes and also caused minor damage to two other occupied mobile homes.

A small grass fire on the 1300 block of Travis Lane in the city of Kaufman killed an elderly man. The grass fire spread to a nearby mobile home, engulfing the home in flames. Two other family members at the residence were injured.
An animal on a power line sparked a grass fire that spread and destroyed one home, four vehicles, and five sheds.

The Manton Fire began in southern Clay County 3 miles south of Bellevue but spread northeast into Montague County. The fire jumped FM 174 west of Bowie then moved over Highway 287 northwest of Bowie. Highway 287 was closed for some time. About 5000 acres burned in this fire.

A fire began near Highway 287 in Mildred but spread west toward the town of Navarro. The fire burned a train tressel that continued to burn for several hours. The fire also burned at least one boat, a travel trailer, and some carpentry equipment. Approximately 35 acres were burned in this fire. This was one of about 10 grass fires that erupted in the county on this day. The fire was contained on the 5th and controlled on the 7th.
A fire near Dawson burned 500 acres. This was one of about 10 grass fires that erupted in the county on this day.
A fire near I-30, FM 1565, and CR 2596 near Royse City burned 75-100 acres and also burned 5 sheds and slightly damaged 2 mobile homes.
Large tree limbs were blown down due to high winds.
A 60 MPH wind gust was reported near Joe Pool Lake.
A 70 MPH wind gust was reported in Seagoville.
A large tree was split at the base due to high winds.
A large tree was blown down along Farm-to-Market Road 1991 east of Clifton.
Thunderstorm winds were estimated to be near 60 MPH. Power outages were also reported.
Large tree limbs were blown down in residential areas of Gun Barrel City.
Large tree limbs were blown down on County Road 1114 near the Johnson County line.
Large tree branches and power lines were blown down due to high winds.
A large tree was blown down along County Road 1450 WSW of Itasca.
A large tree was blown down along County Road 4247 south of Itasca.
A large tree was blown down east of Marlin.
The Texas DEM reported a 2-acre grass fire in the county destroyed a mobile home.
The Texas DEM reported a 25-acre grass fire along FM 219 near Hico destroyed 5 outbuildings and damaged a garage and a house.
The Ireland Fire burned 1023 acres. The fire began near CR 102 and FM 932 and threatened the community of Ireland. One abandoned home was destroyed.
A 600-acre grass fire burned in southwest Hopkins County near the Miller Grove area. The fire began near FM 1567 and burned pastureland and woodland.
Large trees and tree limbs were also blown down along Alamo Road south of Montague. Several of these trees were rotted inside.
Sixty-one mph wind gusts were measured for 5 minutes at Meacham Airport (KFTW) in north Fort Worth.
A 63 mph wind gust was recorded by the RSOIS equipment at the NWS Fort Worth Forecast Office.
Golfball sized hail was reported in Sivells Bend.
Penny sized hail was reported at the Dallas North Tollway and Highway 190 in Plano.
Penny sized hail was reported in Runaway Bay.
Pea to dime sized hail was reported in Benbrook.
Pea to nickel sized hail was reported near I-20 and Hulen St in Fort Worth.
Nickel sized hail was reported near Edgecliff Village.
Quarter sized hail was reported 1 mile north of Edgecliff Village.
Dime to quarter sized hail was reported in north Mansfield.
A 3000-acre fire in western Limestone County began approximately 20 miles east of Waco. This fire burned one home.

Lightning struck the bell tower of the Allen Chapel AME Church on Elm Street, damaging the tower and causing the bricks to tumble onto 1st Street below. The street remained closed for at least 2 days. The church's roof was also damaged.
Severe thunderstorm winds knocked down large trees and large tree branches in Murphy. Also, several power poles were either snapped or leaning in the city.

The roof and door of a large barn along Duncanville Road in Cedar Hill was torn off by severe thunderstorm winds. Trees in the area were also knocked down. Another home in the area also received extensive wind damage. Officials reported about 2 dozen barns and homes in the area has some type of wind damage.
Thunderstorms winds damaged the roof of a house and the roof of a barn.  A tree was also uprooted.
Penny sized hail fell at the intersection of Gray Road and Farm-to-Market 2849, or about 5 miles northwest of Nocona.
Nickel sized hail fell at the intersection of Gray Road and Farm-to-Market 2849, or about 5 miles northwest of Nocona.
Ping pong ball sized hail fell at the intersection of Gray Road and Farm-to-Market 2849, or about 5 miles northwest of Nocona.
An 18-wheeler was blown over by thunderstorm winds in the city of Bonham.
Golfball sized hail was reported at Nocona General Hospital.
A wind gust of 59 MPH was reported by the automated weather station at Cox Field (KPRX).
The roof was blown off the Wolfe City Fire Department building and another building downtown. Trees were also blown over by the thunderstorm winds.
A 70 MPH wind gust was reported near the intersection of West Spring Creek Parkway and Coit Road in Plano.
Penny sized hail was reported covering the ground 3 miles southwest of McKinney.
A 70 MPH wind gust was reported by a trained spotter in Rowlett.
Quarter sized hail was reported by a trained spotter at the intersection of North Shiloh Road and West Buckingham Road in Garland.
A tree, 50 feet tall and 3 feet in diameter, was blown down onto a house in Mesquite.

A 70 MPH wind gust was reported in Garland by a trained spotter.  Limbs up to 5 inches in diameter were knocked down and hail covered the ground. In addition, the strong winds knocked a Chick-Fil-A cow off a billboard along LBJ Freeway in Garland. One accident occurred due to the debris on the highway.
Hail up to the size of quarters fell for several minutes in Garland. In some places, the hail completely covered the ground.  A skylight was damaged by the hail.
Quarter sized hail was reported by a trained spotter in Garrett.
Quarter sized hail was reported by emergency management just south of Rice.
Quarter sized hail was reported in Bristol.
Nickel sized hail was reported along Douglas Street in Garland.
Tree branches were covering the road along Douglas Street in Garland. At least two tree branches fell on cars, damaging two cars.
Trees and small tree branches were knocked down in Frisco. One weeping willow tree was uprooted in a backyard, knocking down the privacy fence.
Strong winds around 40 mph knocked down the Chili's sign in Ennis. The sign fell on the roof of the restaurant, damaging the roof. The strong winds occurred as a cold front moved through the area.

Nearly 19 hours of continuous rain resulted in the flooding of low-lying areas across Hood County. During the evening hours, many low-lying areas in Tolar and Lipan had to be barricaded. The Sheriff's Office reported that the water was nearly 2 feet deep in a few low-lying areas.

High water rescues were needed in Haltom City at Highway 121 and Midway Road. Fossil Creek rose out of its banks covering the intersection in an estimated two feet of water. Two drivers had to be rescued from their vehicles and another two were able to walk to higher ground.
Lightning struck an oil field along I-35 between Gainesville and Valley View, igniting a tank battery on fire.

Nearly 19 hours of continuous rain resulted in widespread nuisance and low-lying flooding across the county. The county received an average of 3-4 of rain during this event. Several creeks and streams overflowed their banks, flooding the surrounding lands and roads. The local newspaper reported that several roads near Clear, Denton, and Hickory creeks had to be barricaded due to high water. Two streets near the University of North Texas campus had to be closed due to localized flooding, and a school bus stalled in high water along South Bonnie Brae Street in the city of Denton. In addition, the low-water crossing at Oliver Creek Road near Justin was washed out.

Nearly 7 hours of continuous rain resulted in nuisance and low-lying flooding across Limestone County. The local newspaper reported some roadways were flooded with a few inches of water flowing over parts of US Highway 84 in Mexia. Some of this water ran into homes in downtown Mexia. Water was also flowing across some parts of Highway 84 between Mexia and Groesbeck. One swift water rescue was performed on FM 339 near Ben Hur when a car was swept off the road. Highway 165 in Groesbeck had to be closed under the railroad tracks due to high water, and Frost Creek jumped out of banks and flooded Groesbeck City Park. Two to five inches of rain fell across the county during this event.

Nearly 20 hours of continuous rain resulted in nuisance and low-lying flooding across Hunt County. The county received between 2 to 5 inches of rainfall. The local newspaper reported several people drove into flooded areas and had to be rescued. There were also several minor accidents, but one male was killed on U.S. Highway 69 near Lone Oak when his vehicle hydroplaned and hit a tree. Portions of Stonewall Street between Stanford and Templeton Streets in Greenville were under water.

Nearly 20 hours of continuous rain resulted in nuisance and low-lying flooding across Hopkins County. The county received between 2 to 4 inches of rainfall. The local newspaper reported several county roads were covered with water but these roads typically flood with heavy rain. The roads include: CRs 1119, 1157, 1120, 1127 off FM 2653, and FM 71 west of the Sulphur River. The entrance to Cooper Lake at FM 71 and FM 3505 was also covered with water. In addition, a bridge along FM 69 near the town of Dike was washed out. The bridge was located along FM 69 approximately 4 miles north of FM 1537/Mahoney Road. The bridge was under construction at the time.

A tree fell on a home along FM 69 South, and knocked a hole in the roof of the home. Many of the trees in the county had been weakened or killed by the persistent drought that plagued the region for the previous 15 months.

A culvert along Tank Destroyer Blvd between Clarke Road and Main Street in Copperas Cove was washed out by heavy rainfall. Approximately 2 inches of rain fell in the area. The culvert had been identified as weak back in October, but the damage caused by the  heavy rainfall finally caused the bridge to become impassable. It was estimated that the repairs would take 5-6 months.
Lightning struck a 2-story house on the 10800 block of Stone House Lane in Frisco. The attic and second story of the home were heavily damaged.

Parts of Highway 79 around the town of Gause were closed due to high water. Several people in vehicles got stuck along the highway around Gause, and some people were forced to spend the night in Gause. The water was reported to be waist deep at Highway 79 and FM 2095, where one person had to be helped to safety.

As the water in the town of Gause continued to slowly rise, flood waters entered a few structures, including Coats Grocery and the fire station. Rising waters also caused problems in Thorndale and Rockdale. In Rockdale, a high water rescue was needed after a car got stuck on FM 908 at Brushy Creek. The rising creek flooded over the roadway. Another high water rescue was performed at the intersection of San Jacinto and Post Oak in Rockdale. Flooding also occurred at other usual locations in Rockdale; including the intersections of Highway 79 at Childress, Meadow, and Calhoun, and a low water crossing on East Belton. Other parts of Meadow and San Jacinto were flooded as well. In Thorndale, water was reported over the road in several locations along Highway 79 and flood waters severely damaged FM 486. One person had to be rescued from their vehicle on County Road 446A. Substantial flooding was also reported throughout the Brushy Creek and San Gabriel River bottomlands.

An EF-1 tornado occurred southeast of the city of Joshua. The tornado began near FM 3048 and Buffalo Lane and traveled to the north-northeast before lifting northeast of the intersection of CR 705 and CR 811. One manufactured home sustained extensive damage, and a barn suffered roof damage. Part of the exterior walls of the manufactured home fell outward and the roof was completely lost. Another manufactured home on the same property sustained damage. Across CR 705, a third manufactured home sustained damage to the exterior. The twister also overturned a horse trailer and damaged two riding lawnmowers on this property. The path length was just over a mile long with a maximum width around 60 yards. The maximum winds were estimated to be around 100 mph.

An EF-0 tornado occurred in an unincorporated area just south of Denton. The tornado touched down in a wheat field southeast of the intersection of Country Club Road and Ryan Rd. The tornado was confirmed by photos, radar, and eyewitness evidence.

An EF-0 tornado occurred in the northern portions of Grand Prairie with maximum estimated winds around 85 mph. The tornado began just south of the intersection of Highway 360 and East Avenue K. As the tornado traveled northeast, it damaged the roofs of a few warehouse buildings and a strip mall. It also knocked over some light and electric poles. The tornado lifted just past Westpark Drive with a path length just under a half of a mile.

A brief EF-0 tornado caused damage to a few trees and the roof of one home near Skyline High School in Dallas. The path of the tornado was 0.1 miles long, the width was 25 yards, and the maximum estimated winds were 80 mph.

An EF-0 tornado with maximum estimated around 85 mph occurred in west Irving. The twister damaged a metal awning at a house and uprooted trees along Avenida Loop by the Irving Mall. Continuing to the northeast, the twister damaged part of the roof of the Goodwill store on N Belt Line Rd and blew HVAC units off the rooftop of the store. Wood power poles were leaning near W Rochelle Rd and N Belt Line Rd. Near the end of the track, trees were uprooted and minor damage was noted at Townsell Elementary School. Two air conditioning units at the school were damaged and so was a gas line. The path length was non-continuous and was approximately 1.3 miles long with a narrow width of 30 yards.

An EF-0 tornado with maximum estimated winds around 80 mph produced damage in the city of Coppell. The tornado began near the intersection of E Belt Line Rd and S Denton Tap Rd. The awning at a gas station was damaged at this intersection. The tornado moved to the northeast through a residential area causing minor damage to some roofs of homes and businesses and also damaging trees. The total path of the tornado was 2 miles long, but the damage path was non-continuous. The damage path was also narrow at about 75 yards wide.
Small tree branches were broken by RFD winds associated with a tornadic supercell near the intersection of Airline Dr and Executive Dr in Coppell.
RFD winds associated with a tornadic supercell ripped shingles off a church near E Belt Line Rd and Ingle Way in Coppell. Some letters from the church sign were also removed.
A very brief tornado touched down in open field near FM 3389 and CR 1170, south of Brashear.

Trained storm spotters reported a tornado 6 miles northwest of Winnsboro which is also about 2 miles southeast of Pickton. The tornado damaged a few trees. Maximum wind speeds were likely around 80 mph.
Damaging thunderstorm winds, likely associated with the RFD of a tornadic supercell, removed some metal panels from the roof of a motel near Highway 183 and Estrada Pkwy in Irving.

An EF-0 tornado with maximum estimated winds around 85 mph occurred in Mesquite. The tornado began near Independence Drive and Meadow Lane then tracked east. Minor roof damage was noted along the track of the tornado and several large trees were split or had large branches broken off. Near the end of the track on the east side of N Galloway Ave, a car service station sustained significant damage. The winds from the tornado penetrated the building through the large service doors. The roof was ripped off the building and the back wall collapsed. The path length of this tornado was 0.3 miles with a width of about 30 yards. Two people sustained minor injuries.
A brief tornado was observed south of Interstate 30 between Campbell and Cumby. This tornado occurred in open country and was rated at EF-0.

Trained spotters and Sulphur Springs PD reported a tornado near Highway 19 North and Loop 301 on the north side of town. This tornado touched down in open country but did damage to a few power poles, power lines, and trees. The tornado was rated an EF-0 with maximum estimated winds near 85 mph. The total path length was around 0.6 miles long with a width of approximately 50 yards.

Several trained storm spotters observed and reported a tornado over open country approximately 6 miles south of Greenville. This EF-0 tornado had maximum estimated winds of approximately 80 mph, a path length of approximately half a mile, and a path width of 50 yards.

An EF-3 tornado did extensive damage as it wound its way through the town of Forney. The tornado began near the intersection of Broad St and N Bois D'arc Street just southwest of Highway 80. As it moved to the northeast, the first significant damage was noted near Aimee St and N Bois D'arc St. There was substantial tree damage with some large trees uprooted near this intersection. Also, shingle damage, roof damage to a fire station nearby, blown out windows at a few homes and an outbuilding was destroyed, all near this intersection.  A street sign at the intersection was also completely bent flat near the base. The tornado moved northeast and crossed Hwy 80 near the Forney Cleaners business where substantial roof and commercial sign damage occurred.  Debris was also observed in the median between the east and westbound lanes near this location. The tornado continued northeast producing light damage to industrial buildings, but was largely over open fields. The tornado then crossed over Ridgecrest Rd and produced substantial damage to many homes in the Diamond Creek subdivision. One of the first homes struck was on Woodberry Dr and was completely destroyed.  Several more homes were destroyed in this subdivision and other homes sustained substantial damage. It was determined that several of the destroyed homes were destroyed as the result of excessive lift being forced upon the roof, and the roofs of these homes were poorly attached to the external walls of the home. Once the roofs failed, pressure built up on internal walls causing the failure of nearly all external and internal walls. As the tornado continued northeast through the subdivision it consistently produced damage to homes, most of which was different degrees of roof or top floor damage. The tornado exited the subdivision at Crosby Elementary School. The tornado damaged several vehicles that were in the school���s parking lot. One vehicle was lofted approximately 300 yards into a field northeast of the school. The school itself sustained mainly roof damage.  Children were in the school when the tornado struck, but no injuries occurred.  The tornado continued northeast for several miles, producing light/EF-0 damage along the way. In total, this tornado destroyed 14 homes, caused major damage to 28 homes and minor damage to another 42 homes. Many of the damaged homes were in the Diamond Creek Subdivision. Due to damage in the Diamond Creek Subdivision, the maximum estimated winds with this tornado were 150 mph. The path length was approximately 7.7 miles, and the maximum width was 150 yards. Seven people sustained non life-threatening injuries.

An EF-3 tornado began in eastern Rockwall County and traveled northeast into Hunt County before lifting. The tornado touched down to the southwest of the intersection of FM 548 and Bent Rd in Rockwall County. The tornado quickly moved into a subdivision and severely damaged or destroyed several homes. The worst of the damage in this subdivision occurred along Laci Ln. Trees and shrubs northeast of these houses by a half mile or so were completely debarked and had no vegetation remaining. The tornado continued northeast and produced damage to homes along Country Manor Rd. There was one house that had a large portion of its roof/top story completely removed.  A couple of small barns were also destroyed, one which contained a classic car which ended up blown into the back of a neighbor���s house. The tornado continued northeast where it crossed Hwy 276 and sideswiped a cabinet factory. Part of the outside metal walls were crumbled. There was an incredible amount of industrial debris downstream of this factory north of the highway. The tornado continued northeast and demolished one mobile home and damaged another right at the Rockwall/Hunt County line. In total, 8 homes in Rockwall County were deemed destroyed, 17 sustained major damage, and 8 sustained minor damage. The path length of the tornado in Rockwall County was nearly 2.4 miles, but the total path length was 3.3 miles. Maximum estimated winds were 150 mph and the tornado was approximately 400 yards wide. Three people sustained minor injuries when their doublewide mobile home was struck near the Rockwall/Hunt County line.

A strong EF-2 tornado began in eastern Rockwall County and traveled northeast into Hunt County before lifting. As the tornado crossed into Hunt County, it destroyed one mobile home near the Rockwall/Hunt County Line. The tornado then continued to the northeast where it destroyed the roof of one more home before lifting north of Highway 276. The path length of the tornado in Hunt County was nearly a mile long, but the total path length was 3.3 miles. Maximum estimated winds with the tornado while it was in Hunt County were likely around 130 mph and the tornado was approximately 400 yards wide.

A tornado began near Highland Road, east of I-35 in Red Oak and continued northeast into Dallas County. The tornado did minor EF-0 damage to trees, crops, and shingles while moving northeast through Ellis County. After the tornado crossed into Dallas County it strengthened and did more substantial damage in the city of Lancaster. The path length of the tornado in Ellis County was approximately 4.4 miles long, but the total path length was 13.7 miles long.

This tornado is a continuation from Ellis County. The tornado crossed into Dallas County near I-35E at the Ellis/Dallas County line. Light damage was noted as the tornado crossed into the county but then the tornado moved into the city of Lancaster and struck the Portofino Apartments where it damaged the roofs of two buildings and tore the roof off another building. Cars were moved in the parking lots, and the windows were blown out in one car. The tornado did significant damage to homes just northeast of the apartment complex, beginning on Sunny Meadow Dr. However, the most significant damage occurred near the intersections of Wintergreen Rd, Telephone Rd, and North Dallas Ave. Many homes in this area were heavily damaged or destroyed. Some cars were pushed into fences, many trees and tree branches were knocked down, an RV was crumpled, and some fence boards penetrated homes. The Cedar Valley Christian Academy also sustained heavy damage when it lost an entire wall. The tornado continued northeast crossing Interstate 20 near Dynasty Drive. The tornado hit a trucking company along the interstate, lofting several empty semis into the air. About 50 semitrailers were damaged or destroyed. The tornado damaged a few additional trees northeast of the trucking company and caused some minor roof damage in the Stagecoach neighborhood. The damage track ended near Palm Island St and Tioga St. In the city of Lancaster, 64 homes were destroyed, 51 sustained major damage, and another 58 sustained minor damage. An additional two homes were destroyed in the Dallas city limits. One home was destroyed when one of the semis from the trucking company was thrown into the house. The path length of the tornado in Dallas County was approximately 9.4 miles long but the total length of the tornado was 13.7 miles. Maximum estimated winds were 130 mph with a maximum width of 200 yards. Ten people in the city of Lancaster were injured, and two people sustained serious injuries.

An EF-2 tornado began in Kennedale, and then moved north-northeast into Arlington. In its occlusion phase, the tornado curved back to the northwest; ending its track near the east shores of Lake Arlington along Waterview Drive. The path length of the tornado was 6.4 miles long with a width of approximately 150 yards.  Damage from the tornado began near the Texas Raceway. Five manufactured homes were heavily damaged or destroyed near the racing strip. Moving to the north-northeast, the tornado produced sporadic damage to trees, power poles, and a storage facility as the storm organized rapidly. Part of the roof of a warehouse at a business on Tower Drive near Business 287 was torn off and tossed onto a city water tower nearby. The warehouse was also damaged by debris tossed by the tornado. Other businesses near this intersection were also damaged. Damage to residences began north of Sublett Rd. EF-2 damage was noted to a few homes between Sublett Rd and Hwy 287, but most areas received EF-0 or EF-1 damage. Approximately 143 homes and apartments sustained some type of damage in this area. Most of the homes appeared to have the initial failure at or near the garage, with subsequent damage coming to exterior walls or portions of roofs. Before the tornado crossed Hwy 287, it damaged the roofs of two buildings at the Chesterfield Apartments. Once the tornado crossed Hwy 287, it cut a path to the north-northeast causing mostly minor roof and fence damage to approximately 25-30 homes between Hwy 287 and Interstate 20. The tornado crossed Interstate 20 between Kelly Elliott Rd and Green Oaks Blvd. First the tornado damaged a church on the north side of the interstate, then the tornado went on to do significant damage in the Oldfield neighborhood just north of Interstate 20 near Martin High School. Approximately 100 homes were damaged in this neighborhood with an additional 85 damaged in the surrounding areas. Several homes experienced significant damage to garages and progressive failure of garage walls and portions of roofs. A few residences in this neighborhood along Haverford Dr and Thorncliffe Dr sustained EF-2 damage. Large trees were also uprooted in the neighborhood. The damage path continued to the north from this area with several other homes and trees sustaining damage near Little Road. Just west of Martin High School, the tornado began to occlude and turn northwest. At this point, near Green Oaks Boulevard and Chaperito Street, a nursing home suffered significant roof and outside wall damage, with the initial failure occurring near a large window. Nearly all of the residential damage in Kennedale and Arlington was EF-0 or EF-1. Only a small portion of the damage path suffered EF-2 damage. A total of 5 homes in Kennedale and 13 homes in Arlington were determined to be destroyed. Another 44 homes sustained major damage and 247 sustained minor damage. An additional 273 residences were affected by the storms on this day. Maximum estimated winds with the tornado were 135 mph. Eight people sustained injuries from the tornado, but only one of those injured was considered severe.

A grassfire burned approximately 750 acres between Pilot Point and Celina in Denton County. The fire began south of FM 455 near Tischler and Riley Road from a tractor that was cutting wheat. Two barns were destroyed in the fire, and two homes were also damaged.

An elderly man was killed when the pile of brush he was burning at his home near Lowry Crossing got out of control. The fire consumed the man. The winds on this morning were approximately 15 to 25 mph with gusts up to 30 mph. A Red Flag Warning was not in effect this day, but the county was under a No Burn Day.

Thunderstorm winds peeled the roof off the intake area at the Milano Livestock Exchange. Several trees were also knocked down by the strong winds. Many of the trees were likely already weakened by the extreme drought that had plagued the county over the past year.

Hail caused significant roof damage in the historic Swiss Avenue neighborhood of Old East Dallas. The hail size was estimated based on surrounding hail reports. One home alone sustained approximately $100,000 in roof damage. Many of the historic homes were rumored to have the original tiling restored on the roofs.
Dime to golf ball sized hail was reported in Celeste.

A brief EF-0 tornado occurred approximately one mile north of Randolph near the intersection of CR 4145 and CR 4160. The tornado caused minor damage to at least one home, large trees, barns, and crops. The maximum winds in the tornado were estimated to be 85 mph.

Damaging downburst winds between 70 to 95 mph caused damage along a line from approximately 1.5 miles north of Randolph to 2 miles east-southeast of Leonard. Many trees were snapped or uprooted along the path and several barns and outbuildings either lost much of their roofs or were overturned. Four manufactured homes were rolled over along the path of destructive winds, and a few more homes sustained damage to the roofs and/or siding. The homes that rolled over were located near FM 1553 and CR 4709 north of Leonard, near CR 4860 and 4855 east of Leonard, and two homes rolled over on CR 4851 east of Leonard. A total of three people were injured from the rolling homes. In addition, the roofs of several buildings in Randolph were partially torn off.

Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down 2-3 tree branches along West Kennedale Pkwy. At a business in the 700 block of West Kennedale Pkwy, some trim was removed from the building, street signs were turned around, and an office door was sucked open. Power lines were also knocked down in the area.

Strong thunderstorm winds damaged a manufactured home near Rogers. Part of the siding of the home was ripped off and part of the metal roof was peeled back.
A Cessna 172 airplane at Waco Regional Airport (KACT) was flipped over due to high winds. The plane was not tied down, and the ASOS at the airport reported a corresponding wind gust of 51 MPH.
Penny hail was reported approximately 9 miles northeast of Kaufman.
Many large tree limbs were blown down on several streets in Belton.

Outflow from thunderstorms to the east produced wind gusts in excess of 45 MPH on the campus of The University of Texas-Dallas, in the city of Richardson. This outflow caused the collapse of a crane which was being dismantled at a construction project. Two workers, a 58 year old male, and a 50 year old male died in the crane collapse.

Waxahachie Fire Department reported that 5 houses were struck by lightning around 8 PM CDT in the city of Waxahachie. Four of the houses caught fire with varying amounts of damage. One home suffered $80,000 worth of damage, while another house only had minor damage and suffered $1,000 worth of damage. The two other homes suffered $150,000 and $40,000 of damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew over an 18 wheeler truck on State Highway 114 in Tarrant County. This occurred just north of the Dallas-Fort Worth International airport (KDFW).

The Anderson County Sheriff reported two oilfield storage tanks were struck by lightning, causing both tanks to catch fire. The tanks were along Anderson County roads 187 and 1224, near State Highway 294.
Power poles were knocked down, trees were snapped and blown over, and minor roof damage occurred to properties.

A three-year-old boy was found inside a day care van during the afternoon hours and died shortly later. The child was left inside the van for at least two hours, and temperatures at the time were near 106 degrees. This occurred at the intersection of Buckner Boulevard and Cordell Drive. The medical examiner determined the cause of death to be heat/hyperthermia.

Outflow from thunderstorms to the east produced wind gusts in excess of 45 MPH on Lake Lewisville. Two men drowned in separate incidents shortly after the strong winds affected the lake. One died after his small inflatable boat overturned from the gusty winds. The other died after he was overcome on his paddle board by choppy waters.

Two teenage brothers drowned at Lake Lewisville after 40 MPH outflow winds moved across the lake. The boys were swimming at the time and one brother was swept out due to the strong winds. The other went out to help him. Both boys were recovered that evening by dive teams.

Northwest Highway at Hillcrest Road was closed due to high water. It was also reported that several cars were flooded out in several streets in the northeast portions of Dallas. Rainfall totals as high as 2 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event.
Multiple roads were being closed in Downtown Dallas due to flash flooding. Rainfall totals as high as 2 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event.

Hall Street by Baylor Hospital in Dallas was flooded due to flash flooding. One fire truck and several vehicles parked on the street stalled in this area. Water also inundated the hospital parking garage where about 20 vehicles were damaged by the rising waters. Rainfall totals as high as 2-2.25 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event.
Law enforcement reported tree damage in Cooper.
Law enforcement reported large trees blown down throughout the city of Sulphur Springs.
A storm spotter reported a 67 mph wind gust.
A wind gust of 73 MPH was measured at the Dallas/Fort Worth National Weather Service Forecast Office.
A wind gust of 67 MPH was measured at the Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base (KNFW). Large tree limbs and at least one power pole was knocked down.
A storm spotter reported an 80 MPH wind gust 4 miles northeast of Venus.
A 69 MPH wind gust was measure at the Comanche County Airport (KMKN).

The Rhodes Ranch II fire was started on the Rhodes Ranch property northeast of the city of Palo Pinto. The fire was started by lightning and burned a total of 1,995 acres. No damage was caused by this fire.

The Dark Valley Ranch fire was started off State Highway 254, east of State Highway 16 between Graford and Possum Kingdom Lake. The fire was started by lightning and burned a total of 1,745 acres. The only damage caused by this fire was to a well site.
A spark from a hay baler started a small grass fire on Blue Flat Road near the Erath County line. The fire burned about 5 acres and burned 4-5 bales of hay.
A church that was being built on Erby Campbell Blvd in Royse City was knocked down by strong thunderstorm winds. Only the wood frame of the building was in place at the time.

Numerous high water rescues were reported around the city of Dallas as the roadways filled with water from heavy rainfall. Rainfall totals as high as 2 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event. It was also reported that the entrance to Dallas Love Field (KDAL) was closed due to high water. A 38-year old male drowned while attempting to fish in White Rock Creek near Samuell Blvd and Interstate 30 in East Dallas. The man was attempting to cross the creek, slipped, and fell into the rapidly flowing creek.

A creek near Alta Vista Road and Keller Haslet Road in north Fort Worth overflowed its banks. A bridge near the intersection was impassable. Rainfall totals as high as 2 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event.
Highway 114 near the Texas Motor Speedway was flooded under Highway 156. Rainfall totals as high as 2 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event.

Four people were trapped in high water under the railroad bridge near Byron Nelson Blvd and Highway 377 in Roanoke. Rainfall totals as high as 2 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event.

Several cars were stalled near West Vickery Blvd and Clover Lane in southwest Fort Worth. High water was also reported at Hulen Street and I-30, Hulen St and Camp Bowie Blvd, and Bledsoe and Currie streets. Rainfall totals as high as 2 in 30 minutes were measured during the heavy rain event.
Flash flooding closed Highway 377 in Keller, approximately 1/4 mile north of Keller Haslet Road.

Areal flooding continued for several hours after scattered to numerous thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall produced flash flooding in the cities of Dallas and Irving. Up to 3.5 of rain had fallen over the city; resulting in the flooding of several streets and creeks. During the evening hours, part of the roof at the Urban Inter-Tribal Center of Texas in the Oak Cliff area collapsed under the weight of the heavy rain that had fallen earlier. As the roof collapsed, the windows in the front blew out.

Areal flooding continued for several hours after scattered to numerous thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall produced flash flooding in Tarrant County. Most of the areal flooding occurred over the northern half of the county. Between 1-4.5 of rain had fallen over the area; resulting in the flooding of several creeks, underpasses, and streets. At about 10:15 pm CDT, a 33-year old man drowned in a swift moving creek near Trammel Davis Road and South Norwood Drive in Fort Worth. The man stepped into the creek to cool off and was swept off his feet.

Areal flooding continued for several hours after scattered to numerous thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall produced flash flooding in southern Denton County. Between 1-3 of rain had fallen over the area; resulting in the flooding of several creeks, underpasses, and streets.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a steel roof and metal rack onto 3 vehicles, damaging the cars.

Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms throughout the day produced rain-slicked roads across the area. According to the Texas Department of Public Service in McLennan County, 13 minor accidents were reported along I-35 in the county. Five people were transported to the hospital with minor injuries.

Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms throughout the day produced rain-slicked roads across the area. A three-vehicle accident occurred in Glen Rose near the Sonic Drive-In. Three people were sent to the hospital; one in critical condition. The cause of the accident was hydroplaning due to heavy rain at the time.
Lightning struck Rednecks Bait and Tackle in Crowley, setting fire to part of the store. The bolt also struck the owner who was inside the shop at the time. The man was checked on scene and released.

Heavy rainfall flooded Trinity View Park and its parking lot, trapping a few visitors in the park. Several cars were flooded up to the door of the car, and three visitors had to be rescued by the Fire Department.

A grass fire burned approximately 440 acres in Unit 21 of the LBJ National Grasslands. The fire was started on the 12th when lightning struck a tree, but the fire violently ignited just before noon on the 13th as temperatures rose into the mid and upper 90s. The fire was burning near CR 2690 northeast of Alvord. According to the Southern Area Coordination Center, the fire was out by the 15th.

A 300-acre grass fire burned near the Slocum Ranch area near Cresson. Above average temperatures near 100 degrees and low humidity values in the 20s resulted in elevated fire weather conditions on this day.

A 12-acre fire near Springtown burned three homes and a barn. The fire began near Carter Road and FM 51.  Above average temperatures over 100 degrees and low humidity values in the teens resulted in elevated fire weather conditions on this day.

A 250-acre grass fire between Keene and Cleburne burned 3 barns. The fire occurred north of Highway 67, and between CR 801 and Highway 174. A discarded glass bottle ignited the fire after it acted like a magnifying glass on the dry grass. Temperatures on this day were very warm around 105 degrees and humidity values were in the teens.

A wildfire was started just west of Lometa off CR 1610 by lightning from a thunderstorm that moved through the area Sunday night through early Monday (Aug 12-13). This fire was difficult to fight due to the rough terrain and particularly thick brush, and ended up burning around 2,100 acres and forcing the evacuation of 6 homes.

Parker County began the month with severe/D2 drought severity in place. Conditions deteriorated to D3/extreme drought during the second week in December and remained as such through the end of the month.

D2 conditions persisted county-wide at the beginning of the month, while D3 conditions had begun to expand into the northern portions of the county. D3/extreme drought conditions covered the entire county by mid December. Fort Hood military base implemented stage one drought water conservation measures on Tuesday, December 4 and kept them in place for the rest of the month.

Extreme drought conditions plagued the county through the entire month, while D4/exceptional drought conditions began to affect the northwestern portions of the county during the second half of December. Waco Regional Airport received 0.81 inch of rain, which is 1.94 inches below normal for December. Farmers and ranchers felt the effects of the drought in terms of the quality of the winter wheat crop and condition of cattle.

The ongoing severe drought at the beginning of the month deteriorated to extreme/D3 conditions during the second half of the month across the western half of the county. During the second week of December, the Navarro County Commissioners Court enacted a burn ban, which would remain in place through the end of the month.

Extreme/D3 drought conditions expanded from west to east across the county during the first half of December, and remained in place through the end of the month. On Monday, Dec 10, county commissioners unanimously approved a county-wide outdoor burn ban.
